newsitem.title: USA: House ethics panel approves Dole loan to Gingrich.
newsitem.headline: House ethics panel approves Dole loan to Gingrich.

text.p: The House ethics committee Thursday approved a possible loan of up to $150,000 from Bob Dole to House Speaker Newt Gingrich to help the embattled speaker pay a $300,000 penalty for ethics violations.
Seeking to satisfy critics who had charged Gingrich was getting a sweetheart deal from Dole, the speaker also made a first $50,000 payment using personal funds.
"In keeping true to his word to personally reimburse the American people, Speaker Gingrich made an initial payment of $50,000 from his own funds," Gingrich spokeswoman Christina Martin said.

The terms of the proposed loan are more stringent than the original Dole agreement, which stunned Washington when it was announced last month. When the loan was first unveiled April 17, Gingrich was expected to borrow the full $300,000 from former Republican presidential nominee Dole.
Further, Gingrich would not have had to pay off the loan for eight years -- after he planned to retire from Congress -- although interest would have accrued during that time.
Under the new arrangement approved by the ethics panel, Gingrich is scheduled to make additional $50,000 payments on June 1 and Nov. 30, 1998. A final $150,000 payment would be due Jan. 2, 1999.

The speaker could borrow up to $150,000 from Dole at the time the final instalment came due. The loan would have to paid back over five years, beginning Jan. 2, 2000. That is before Gingrich's announced retirement date of 2002.
The loan would carry a 10 percent interest rate.

As collateral, the speaker put up his home in Georgia and proceeds from a second book to be published by HarperCollins Publishing Inc. under an existing contract. That is also tougher than the initial plan.
There had been some question whether the ethics panel, which had to review the terms of the loan, would consider it a gift from Dole.
In a Thursday letter to Gingrich, members of the bipartisan ethics committee said the terms of the loan were "commercially reasonable and in conformance with House rules and standards."
They also said Gingrich was providing more security than normal borrowers would have to offer to receive a commercial loan.
The letter was signed by Republican Chairman James Hansen of Utah and Democratic Representative Howard Berman of California.
The agreement also stipulates that the loan would be have to be replaced with a commercial loan if Dole, who recently joined a big-name Washington law firm, became a lobbyist while it was in effect.

Dole recently joined the law firm of Verner, Liipfert, Bernhard, McPherson and Hand which represents a number of large defence firms and is involved in tobacco issues. Dole has stated that he has no plans to lobby.
Gingrich was the first House speaker ever reprimanded for ethics violations. He was punished for his aggressive use of tax exempt groups to advance his political agenda.

Gingrich insisted he had not intentionally done anything wrong, but failed to safeguard against tax abuses by the groups as well as submitting false and misleading information to the ethics committee. This last charge caused the committee to extend its investigation. The $300,000 penalty was intended to compensate the House for the cost of the inquiry.
Gingrich makes an annual salary of $171,500.
